candidates.name: prepare-single-product-reaction-sequences
candidates.description: Draft procedure for filtering atom-mapped reaction data, splitting related reactions together, and constructing source and target sequences with separate reactant and reagent tokenization.
candidates.operation: Prepare single-product reaction examples for sequence-to-sequence learning, branching on canonicalizability, product count, atom contribution, and membership in the common-reagent vocabulary.

inputs.text: Atom-mapped reaction SMILES containing reactant, reagent, and product groups.

citations.quote:
Such reaction strings are composed of three groups of molecules: the reactants, the reagents, and
 the products, which are separated by a ‘>’ sign.
To prepare the reactions, we ﬁrst used the atom mappings to separate reagents from reactants.

inputs.text: The set of 76 common reagents used to define the reagent vocabulary.

citations.quote:
we employed a reagent-wise tokenization
using a set of the 76 most common reagents

outputs.text: Space-separated source sequences representing reactants followed by common reagents, paired with tokenized single-product targets.

citations.quote:
tokenized “reactants > common reagents” and the target sequence of a tokenized “product”. The
tokens were separated by space characters.

outputs.text: Training, validation, and test partitions in an 18:1:1 ratio, keeping reactions with the same reactants in one partition.

citations.quote:
randomly split into training, validation and test sets (18:1:1)3. Reactions with the same reactants, but
different reagents and products were kept in the same set.

steps.text: Compare reaction strings without atom mapping to remove duplicates; discard reactions whose SMILES cannot be canonicalized with RDKit, and retain only single-product reactions.

citations.quote:
removed 720,768 duplicates by comparing reaction strings without atom mapping and an additional
780 reactions, because the SMILES string could not be canonicalized with RDKit

We took only single
product reactions, corresponding to 92% of the dataset, to have distinct prediction targets.

steps.text: Randomly partition the retained examples in an 18:1:1 ratio, assigning reactions with identical reactants but different reagents or products to the same partition.

citations.quote:
randomly split into training, validation and test sets (18:1:1)3. Reactions with the same reactants, but
different reagents and products were kept in the same set.

steps.text: Use atom mappings to classify an input molecule as a reactant if it contributes atoms to the product; otherwise classify it as a reagent.

citations.quote:
molecules with atoms appearing in the product were classiﬁed as reactants and the others without
atoms in the product as reagents.

steps.text: Remove hydrogen atoms and atom mappings, canonicalize the molecules, and tokenize reactants and products atom-wise using the paper's regular expression.

citations.quote:
Then, we removed the hydrogen atoms and the atom mappings
from the reaction string, and canonicalized the molecules. Afterwards, we tokenized reactants and
products atom-wise using the following regular expression:

steps.text: For reagents in the common-reagent set, append distinct reagent tokens after the first '>' in occurrence order. Remove reagents outside that set.

citations.quote:
this set were added as distinct tokens after the ﬁrst ‘>’ sign, ordered by occurrence. Other reagents,
which were not in the set, were neglected and removed completely from the reaction string.

steps.text: Construct source and target sequences with spaces between tokens and point tokens between individual molecules; apply the same preprocessing to every dataset.

citations.quote:
The tokens are separated by a
space and individual molecules by a point token.

tokenized “reactants > common reagents” and the target sequence of a tokenized “product”. The
tokens were separated by space characters. The preprocessing steps together with examples are
summarized in Table 2.
The same preprocessing steps were applied to all datasets.

candidates.name: predict-reaction-products-with-confidence-abstention
candidates.description: Draft procedure for decoding reaction products, canonicalizing predictions, and abstaining when the top prediction has insufficient probability.
candidates.operation: Use beam-search sequence prediction and a confidence threshold to return a product or an unknown outcome, then assess exact-match accuracy and coverage.

inputs.text: Tokenized reactant and common-reagent source sequences and a trained reaction sequence-to-sequence model.

citations.quote: tokenized “reactants > common reagents” and the target sequence of a tokenized “product”.

After the hyperparameter optimization, we continued to train our best model on the
395,496 reactions in Jin’s USPTO train set and tested the fully trained model on Jin’s USPTO test
set.

inputs.text: A confidence threshold on top-1 beam-search probability; 0.83 is the paper's example threshold.

citations.quote:
A clear difference can be observed and used to deﬁne a threshold under which we
determine that the network does not know what to predict.
For example, for a conﬁdence threshold of 0.83 the

we use full-sequence accuracy, the strictest criteria possible, as our evaluation
metric by which a test prediction is considered correct only if all tokens are identical to the ground
truth.

outputs.text: A canonicalized predicted product for accepted predictions, or an unknown outcome when confidence falls below the threshold.

citations.quote: The ﬁnal step was to canonicalize the network output.

A clear difference can be observed and used to deﬁne a threshold under which we
determine that the network does not know what to predict.

outputs.text: Top-1 accuracy and prediction coverage as functions of the confidence threshold.

citations.quote:
Figure 1b shows the top-1 accuracy and
coverage depending on the conﬁdence threshold.

steps.text: Decode using beam width 10 without a length penalty, retaining the 10 most probable sequences at each time step.

citations.quote:
we used a beam width of 10 without length penalty for the inference. Therefore the 10 most
probable sequences were kept at every time step.

steps.text: Use the top-1 beam-search probability as the confidence signal and canonicalize the network output.

citations.quote:
We used the top-1 probabilities to analyze the prediction
conﬁdence of the network.
The ﬁnal step was to canonicalize the network output.

steps.text: If the top-1 probability is below the selected threshold, classify the outcome as unknown; otherwise retain the prediction. Examine the resulting tradeoff between accuracy and coverage.

citations.quote:
A clear difference can be observed and used to deﬁne a threshold under which we
determine that the network does not know what to predict. Figure 1b shows the top-1 accuracy and
coverage depending on the conﬁdence threshold.

steps.text: Evaluate correctness by full-sequence equality after canonicalization so a correct molecule in noncanonical token order can still count as correct.

citations.quote:
we use full-sequence accuracy, the strictest criteria possible, as our evaluation
metric by which a test prediction is considered correct only if all tokens are identical to the ground
truth.

Thus, molecules that were correctly predicted, but whose
tokens were not enumerated in the canonical order, were still counted as correct.

steps.text: For a full-test-set comparison against models covering multiple-product reactions, count those unsupported reactions as false predictions.

citations.quote:
To make a fair comparison, we count
all the multiple product reactions in the test set as false predictions for our model because we trained
only on the single product reactions.
